In this notebook, we’ll do some cursory runs of SingleR on a couple osteosarcoma samples of varying metadata and compare results when using:

  • the reference that matches its type
  • a concatenated version of these references with cell types between them kept distinct (“concatenated”)
  • a concatenated version of these references with cell types between them merged where they share a label (“harmonized”)

This notebook is therefore very similar to 03a-compare-patient-references-ann-level2.Rmd, except based on observations from that analysis we change the labels we use:

  • We use Ann_Level1 annotations for Tumor and Mesenchymal groups, whose cell types we observed that SingleR struggled to differentiate
  • We use Ann_Level2 annotations for the other groups (Epithelial_Endothelial, Immune_Lymphoid, Immune_Myeloid)

We again compare the same two samples, one primary and one metastasis, which each appear in ScPCA and OsteoCar, since this represents the closest we can get to “ground truth.”

Functions

First we define the run_singler() function, which runs SingleR over a given matched reference as well as the two kinds of combined references and returns them in a list.

# Function to run SingleR for a given SCE for each type of reference we are evaluating here.
# Should operate on `label_combined`
run_singler <- function(
    sce, 
    ref_main,
    ref_title,
    ref_harmonized = harmonized_aggr,
    ref_concatenated = concatenated_aggr
  ) {
    
  # Reference that matches this sample
  res_main <- SingleR::SingleR(
    sce,
    ref_main,
    labels = ref_main$label_combined,
    restrict = intersect(rownames(ref_main), rownames(sce)),
    BPPARAM = bp_param
  )
  
  shared_genes <- intersect(rownames(ref_harmonized), rownames(sce))

  # Harmonized reference
  res_harmonized <- SingleR::SingleR(
    sce,
    ref_harmonized,
    labels = ref_harmonized$label_combined,
    restrict = shared_genes,
    BPPARAM = bp_param
  )
  
  # Concatenated reference
  res_concatenated <- SingleR::SingleR(
    sce,
    ref_concatenated,
    labels = ref_concatenated$label_combined,
    restrict = shared_genes,
    BPPARAM = bp_param
  )

  # return list of results
  # this syntax allows the string that main_title hold to be used as the name
  results <- setNames(
    list(res_main, res_harmonized, res_concatenated),
    c(ref_title, "Harmonized reference", "Concatenated reference")
  )
  return(results)
}

Next we’ll source some utility functions:

  • get_top_n(), a helper function to downsample a SingleR results DataFrame to only the top n cell types in
  • plot_results(), which plots both a barplot of cell type annotation counts as well as a ridge plot of delta.next scores for a SingleR result DataFrame
  • plot_delta_next_per_reference(), which plots the distribution of delta.next scores for matching labels across references from a named list of SingleR results.
  • jaccard(), make_jaccard_df(), and plot_jaccard_heatmap() which are used to prepare a data frame of Jaccard similarity index values between two sets of results and plot this in a heatmap

This notebook defines some functions that are used to explore references. It is generally not meant to be run standalone.

Functions to plot and wrangle the output from SingleR:

# Convert the DataFrame to a data.frame with only the top_n labels in the given label_col
get_top_n <- function(res_dataframe, label_col, top_n = 10) {
  df <- res_dataframe |> 
    as.data.frame() 
  
  # subset to top_n most frequent labels
  top_labels <- df |> 
    dplyr::count({{label_col}}, sort = TRUE) |> 
    dplyr::slice_head(n = top_n) |> 
    dplyr::pull({{label_col}})
  
  # return
  df |> 
    dplyr::filter({{label_col}} %in% top_labels)
  
}

# function to plot annotation counts and delta next scores for top n recovered cell types
plot_results <- function(res_dataframe, plot_title, top_n = 10) {
  df <- get_top_n(res_dataframe, pruned.labels, top_n)
  
  barplot <- ggplot(df) + 
    aes(y = forcats::fct_infreq(pruned.labels)) + 
    geom_bar(fill = "cornflowerblue", color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.25) +
    # put the title here instead of shared via patchwork since apparently that
    # gets overridden when I call plot_annotation() again to wrap all of these
    labs(x = "number of cells", y = "pruned label", title = plot_title) +
    theme_bw(base_size = 8) + 
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 8))
  

  deltanext_plot <- ggplot(df) + 
    aes(x = delta.next, y = forcats::fct_infreq(pruned.labels)) + 
    ggridges::geom_density_ridges(
      fill = "darkslategray", 
      alpha = 0.5, 
      linewidth = 0.25,
      scale = 0.95,
      # show median line
      quantile_lines = TRUE, 
      quantiles = 2, 
      # add rug
      jittered_points = TRUE,
      position = ggridges::position_points_jitter(width = 0, height = 0), # Removes vertical jitter if for a true rug
      point_shape = "|", 
      point_size = 0.2, 
      point_colour = "firebrick"
    ) +
    labs(x = "delta next", y = "pruned label") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 8)
  
  patchwork::wrap_plots(barplot, deltanext_plot)
}

# function to plot the delta.next scores for the top_n cell types for
# cells that have the same annotation across references
plot_delta_next_per_reference <- function(result_list, top_n = 10) {
  combined_results <- result_list |>
    purrr::map(\(res) {
      res |>
        as.data.frame() |>
        tibble::rownames_to_column("barcode") |>
        dplyr::select(barcode, delta.next, pruned.labels) |>
        # for this comparison strip out the prefix
        dplyr::mutate(
          pruned.labels_noprefix = stringr::str_remove(pruned.labels, "^prim_") |>
            stringr::str_remove("^mets_")
        )
    }) |>
    purrr::list_rbind(names_to = "reference") |>
    get_top_n(pruned.labels_noprefix, top_n)
  
  
  same_label_barcodes <- combined_results |>
    dplyr::count(barcode, pruned.labels_noprefix) |>
    dplyr::filter(n == 3) |>
    dplyr::pull(barcode)
  
  # only keep if there are at least times the label appears per reference though
  labels_to_plot <- combined_results |>
    dplyr::filter(barcode %in% same_label_barcodes) |>
    dplyr::count(reference, pruned.labels_noprefix) |>
    dplyr::filter(n >= 3) |>
    dplyr::pull(pruned.labels_noprefix)
  
  combined_results |>
    dplyr::filter(
      barcode %in% same_label_barcodes, 
      pruned.labels_noprefix %in% labels_to_plot
    ) |> 
    ggplot() + 
    aes(x = delta.next, y = reference) + 
    ggridges::geom_density_ridges(
      fill = "lemonchiffon", 
      alpha = 0.5, 
      linewidth = 0.25,
      scale = 0.95,
      # show median line
      quantile_lines = TRUE, 
      quantiles = 2, 
      # add rug
      jittered_points = TRUE,
      position = ggridges::position_points_jitter(width = 0, height = 0), # Removes vertical jitter if for a true rug
      point_shape = "|", 
      point_size = 0.5, 
      point_colour = "chocolate3"
    ) +
    facet_grid(vars(pruned.labels_noprefix)) + 
    theme(
      axis.text =  element_text(size = 6),
      strip.text = element_text(size = 6)
    )
}

Functions to create Jaccard similarity heatmaps:

jaccard <- function(a, b) {
  length(intersect(a, b)) / length(union(a, b))
}


# Make a data frame of jaccard indices that we can use for a ggplot heatmap
make_jaccard_df <- function(labels1, labels2) {
  stopifnot(length(labels1) == length(labels2))
  
  ids <- seq_along(labels1)
  
  labels1 <- ifelse(is.na(labels1), "Unknown", labels1)
  labels2 <- ifelse(is.na(labels2), "Unknown", labels2)
  
  id1_list <- split(ids, labels1)
  id2_list <- split(ids, labels2)
  
  sizes1 <- lengths(id1_list)
  sizes2 <- lengths(id2_list)
  
  cross_df <- tidyr::expand_grid(id1 = names(id1_list), id2 = names(id2_list))
  
  cross_df |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      jaccard = purrr::pmap_dbl(
        cross_df,
        \(id1, id2) jaccard(id1_list[[id1]], id2_list[[id2]])
      ),
      id1_label = glue::glue("{id1} (n={sizes1[id1]})"),
      id2_label = glue::glue("{id2} (n={sizes2[id2]})")
    )
}

plot_jaccard_heatmap <- function(labels1, labels2, labels1_lab, labels2_lab) {
  
  jaccard_df <- make_jaccard_df(labels1, labels2)
  
  ggplot(jaccard_df) +
    aes(
      x = forcats::fct_rev(id1_label),
      y = id2_label,
      fill = jaccard
    ) +
    geom_tile(color = "grey80") +
    scale_fill_distiller(palette = "RdBu", direction = -1, limits = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(x = labels1_lab, y = labels2_lab, fill = "Jaccard") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
}

compare_to_ground_truth <- function(res_dataframe, ground_truth_df) {
  res_dataframe |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    tibble::rownames_to_column("barcode") |>
    dplyr::inner_join(ground_truth_df, by = "barcode") |>
    dplyr::select(pruned.labels, ground_truth_label)
}

Define control samples

We’ll define the samples we’re using here. These were chosen based on manual inspection of how many cells are present and how many barcodes overlap with OsteoCAR to be able to get some decent signal here.

prim_sample <- "SCPCS000813"
mets_sample <- "SCPCS000785"

test_samples <- readr::read_tsv(
  file.path(ref_dir, "SCPCP000023-osteocar-samples.tsv")
) |>
  dplyr::filter(scpca_sample_id %in% c(prim_sample, mets_sample)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    rds_file = file.path(
      data_dir, scpca_project_id, scpca_sample_id, glue::glue("{scpca_library_id}_processed.rds")
    )
  )
test_samples

Read and prepare references

We prepare these references:

  • prim_aggr: Patient primary
  • mets_aggr: Patient metastasis
  • harmonized_aggr: Merged references, where cell type labels are retained. In other words, if both references have T cells, we end up with only a single T cell label in harmonized_aggr
  • concatenated_aggr: Merged references, where cell type labels are prefixed with mets_ and prim_. In other words, if both references have T cells, we end up with two labels in concatenated_aggr, e.g. mets_tcell and prim_tcell

Note that the harmonized_aggr and concatenated_aggr are created from prim_aggr and mets_aggr, because of memory. In other words, the raw references could not be combined on their own.

Read in the SCE-formatted references:

# Read and remove unused counts assay to save a little space
patient_prim <- readr::read_rds(file.path(ref_dir, "patient_prim_sce.rds"))
patient_mets <- readr::read_rds(file.path(ref_dir, "patient_mets_sce.rds"))
counts(patient_prim) <- NULL
counts(patient_mets) <- NULL

Before we aggregate, we’ll grab the ground truth cell types we’re interested in for comparison from the raw reference files. In this case, we’re interested in:

  • All tumor and mesenchymal as defined in Ann_Level1. This means all such cells are, respectively, labeled as just “Tumor” and “Mesenchymal”
  • All other labels are taken from Ann_Level2, which is more fine-grained
extract_ground_truth <- function(ref, submitter_id) {
  colData(ref) |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    tibble::rownames_to_column("cell_id") |>
    # extract the barcode
    dplyr::mutate(
      original_sample_id = stringr::str_remove(cell_id, "_[ACGT]+-1"), 
      barcode = stringr::str_remove(cell_id, original_sample_id) |>
        stringr::str_remove("^_") |>
        stringr::str_remove("-1$")) |>
    dplyr::filter(original_sample_id == submitter_id) |>
    dplyr::mutate(
      ground_truth_label = ifelse(
        Ann_Level1 == "Tumor", 
        "Tumor", 
        Ann_Level2
      ), 
      ground_truth_label = ifelse(
        Ann_Level1 == "Mesenchymal", 
        "Mesenchymal", 
        ground_truth_label
      )
    ) |>
    dplyr::select(original_sample_id, barcode, ground_truth_label, ground_truth_ann_level1 = Ann_Level1) |>
    # nicer printing for dev
    tibble::as_tibble()
}


# Define data frames with "ground truth" cell types
prim_ground_truth <- extract_ground_truth(
  patient_prim, 
  test_samples$submitter_id[test_samples$scpca_sample_id == prim_sample]
)

mets_ground_truth <- extract_ground_truth(
  patient_mets, 
  test_samples$submitter_id[test_samples$scpca_sample_id == mets_sample]
)

Aggregate references:

prim_aggr <- SingleR::aggregateReference(
  ref = patient_prim,
  labels = patient_prim$Ann_Level2,
  ntop = 2000, # use 2000 genes for PCA
  BPPARAM = bp_param
)
mets_aggr <- SingleR::aggregateReference(
  ref = patient_mets,
  labels = patient_mets$Ann_Level2,
  ntop = 2000,
  BPPARAM = bp_param
)

Now we’ll combine the Tumor and Mesenchymal each into one category in the aggregated references. The reason we change these labels after aggregating instead of before is to preserve diversity among those original cell labels and ensure they make equal contributions towards the overall grouping, which would not necessarily be the case if we collapsed the labels before aggregating. That said, this is an analysis choice and exploring its consequences further may be merited.

# all cell types are the same for tumor, but not mesenchymal
label_subtypes <- list(
  "Tumor" = patient_prim$Ann_Level2[patient_prim$Ann_Level1 == "Tumor"] |> unique(), 
  "Mesenchymal" = c(
    patient_prim$Ann_Level2[patient_prim$Ann_Level1 == "Mesenchymal"] |> unique(),
    patient_mets$Ann_Level2[patient_mets$Ann_Level1 == "Mesenchymal"] |> unique()
  ) |> unique()
)


# Helper function to rename the aggregated reference, including both the labels and colnames
# The final label ends up in colData `label_combined`
rename_aggr <- function(ref_aggr, subtype_list = label_subtypes) {
  
  # for loop to modify ref_aggr
  ref_aggr$label_combined <- ref_aggr$label
  for (big_label in names(subtype_list)) {
    ref_aggr$label_combined <- ifelse(
      ref_aggr$label %in% subtype_list[[big_label]],
      big_label,
      ref_aggr$label_combined
    )
  }
  
  colnames(ref_aggr) <- paste0(
    ref_aggr$label_combined, 
    1:length(ref_aggr$label_combined)
  )
  
  ref_aggr
}
prim_aggr <- rename_aggr(prim_aggr)
mets_aggr <- rename_aggr(mets_aggr)

Create the combined references:

shared_genes <- intersect(
  rownames(prim_aggr),
  rownames(mets_aggr)
)

harmonized_aggr <- cbind(
  prim_aggr[shared_genes, ],
  mets_aggr[shared_genes, ]
)

prim_aggr$label_combined <- glue::glue("prim_{prim_aggr$label_combined}")
mets_aggr$label_combined <- glue::glue("mets_{mets_aggr$label_combined}")
concatenated_aggr <- cbind(
  prim_aggr[shared_genes, ],
  mets_aggr[shared_genes, ]
)

# Undo the re-labeling after created the reference above
prim_aggr$label_combined <- stringr::str_remove(prim_aggr$label_combined, "^prim_")
mets_aggr$label_combined <- stringr::str_remove(mets_aggr$label_combined, "^mets_")

As a reminder, what are the cell types as recorded in OsteoCAR?

ggplot(prim_ground_truth) +
  aes(y = forcats::fct_infreq(ground_truth_label)) + 
  geom_bar(fill = "darksalmon", color = "grey20") + 
  facet_grid(vars(ground_truth_ann_level1), scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "count", y = "cell type") +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 7))

75% of the SCE cells are in OsteoCAR, and the vast majority of them are types of tumor cells.

Next, we’ll run SingleR:

results <- run_singler(
  sce,
  ref_main = prim_aggr,
  ref_title = "Primary patient reference"
) |>
  # convert the NA label to Unknown
  purrr::map(
    \(res) {
      res$pruned.labels[is.na(res$pruned.labels)] <- "Unknown"
      res
    }
  )

Annotated cell types

The following plots show the distribution of cell types annotated for each reference as well as distributions of the delta.next scores.

purrr::imap(results, plot_results) |>
  patchwork::wrap_plots(nrow = 3) + patchwork::plot_annotation(title = "Primary patient sample") 
Picking joint bandwidth of 0.00717
Picking joint bandwidth of 0.00634
Picking joint bandwidth of 0.00569

We see that the Tumor delta.next scores are all much higher than what we previously observed in the 03a notebook, suggesting that combining this into a single category is giving us higher confidence to label malignant cells. But, it is notable that the Mesenchymal category still has low associated delta.next values. Endothelial and TAMs are bimodal, suggesting some labels are more confident than others. More interestingly, mesenchymal cells are only really coming back for the harmonized reference, and not for the matched primary or the concatenated reference. This reference is also able to detect a handful of epithelial cells, which aren’t seen for the matched primary reference because that cell type isn’t in the primary reference!

Next, we’ll plot the distributions of delta.next scores shown for cells which have the same annotation (ignoring the primary/mets source!) across all three references. The plot considers only the top 10 cell types (if there are that many in common), and only plots cell types with at least 3 cells per reference. This will show us if any of the references is more confidently assigning these cell types.

plot_delta_next_per_reference(results)

The Tumor cell delta.next values tend to be higher for the matched (primary) reference, and also with a long right tail and is not bimodal with a set of lower-confidence calls. This actually points towards using the primary reference only.

SingleR heatmaps

SingleR::plotScoreHeatmap(results$`Primary patient reference`, main = "Primary patient reference")

SingleR::plotScoreHeatmap(results$`Harmonized reference`, main = "Harmonized reference")

SingleR::plotScoreHeatmap(results$`Concatenated reference`, main = "Concatenated reference")

The same general pattern is present all around: Tumor is the clear main label for all references, and there is decent signal for both Mesenchymal and Endothelial cells throughout as well. The signal for Mesenchymal cells is much stronger for the combined references.

Jaccard heatmaps for ground truth comparisons

Next, we’ll look at some comparisons between these calls and the “ground truth” labels, which are the labels that the overlapping barcodes have in these inferences and in the OsteoCAR reference itself. We’ll make some Jaccard heatmaps, where the OsteoCAR annotations are shown on the x-axis.

results |>
  purrr::imap(
    \(res, res_name) {
      compare_df <- compare_to_ground_truth(res, prim_ground_truth)
      plot_jaccard_heatmap(
        compare_df$ground_truth_label,
        compare_df$pruned.labels, 
        "",
        res_name
      )
    }
  ) |>
  patchwork::wrap_plots(ncol = 1)

These heatmaps show some pretty good agreement with tumor cell and endothelial cells, but less so mesenchymal cells. Even for the harmonized reference where these cells are identified, it’s not a very good match to the ground truth labels, so it’s not clear if it’s actually a “good” thing that those labels were assigned.

We see a flip here between the matched metastasis reference and the combined references: for the matched reference, most cells are mesenchymal, then TAMs, and then tumor. For the combined references, we see most are Tumor, then TAMs, and far fewer mesenchymal.

Looking at the delta.next scores, these seem to be generally higher for the matched metastasis reference compared to the combined references.

Next, we’ll plot the distributions of delta.next scores shown for the top 10 cell types which have the same annotation (ignoring the primary/mets source!) across all three references. This will show us if any of the references is more confidently assigning these cell types.

plot_delta_next_per_reference(results)

There’s not much of a strong trend here; median values look about the same for each set of delta.next distributions, but it’s worth noting that the mesenchymal delta.next appears larger for the matched metastasis reference vs the combined. We also see a couple cases where concatenated delta.next values might be a bit lower, but again it’s not a strong or definitive trend.

SingleR heatmaps

SingleR::plotScoreHeatmap(results$`Metastasis patient reference`, main = "Metastasis patient reference")

SingleR::plotScoreHeatmap(results$`Harmonized reference`, main = "Harmonized reference")

SingleR::plotScoreHeatmap(results$`Concatenated reference`, main = "Concatenated reference")

Across all references, tumor and mesenchymal categories are coming back with high scores for the same groups of cells, which is expected from earlier plots. Importantly, TAMs does not have interplay with either of those cell types (which makes sense biologically!).

Jaccard heatmaps for ground truth comparisons

Next, we’ll ask how these results compare to ground truth.

results |>
  purrr::imap(
    \(res, res_name) {
      compare_df <- compare_to_ground_truth(res, mets_ground_truth)
      plot_jaccard_heatmap(
        compare_df$ground_truth_label,
        compare_df$pruned.labels, 
        "",
        res_name
      )
    }
  ) |>
  patchwork::wrap_plots(ncol = 1)

Cells that are mesenchymal in the ground truth are generally called as tumor cells in the metastasis reference, but they tend to be more accurately called as mesenchymal for the combined references.

Conclusions

Based on these results, it seems reasonable to proceed with a harmonized reference (aka, labels fully combined between references). The main item pointing against that was the higher tumor delta.next for the primary reference, but tumor annotations were fairly consistent across references so this is not an argument against using a harmonized reference. But, we will likely want to dig deeper into the precise construction of that reference, including:

  • Whether we should downsample and combine before aggregating
  • Whether we should be summarizing cell types into broad “mesenchymal” and “tumor” categories before or after aggregating
